lesson.title: Medical Terminology: Foundations and Oncology Focus

pages.title: Part 1, Page 1: Medical Terms Are Built, Not Memorized

content.text: Medical language looks intimidating until you realize it's built from a small, reusable set of pieces — mostly derived from Greek and Latin — combined the same way every time. Once you know the pieces, you can decode terms you've never seen before, rather than memorizing an endless vocabulary list.
Every medical term is built from some combination of: a

(attached to the end, often indicating a condition or procedure), and sometimes a
(usually "o") that links pieces together for pronunciation.

pages.title: Part 1, Page 5: Decoding a Real Term

content.text: Let's put the pieces together. Take the word
This is the whole skill in a nutshell: break an unfamiliar term into its pieces, translate each piece, and reassemble the meaning — no memorization of the whole word required.
Break down "hepatomegaly": hepat/o (liver) + -megaly (enlargement). What does it mean?
Hepat/o = liver, -megaly = enlargement, so hepatomegaly literally means "enlarged liver."

Knowing this hierarchy helps you place any new term in context — is it describing something at the cellular level, or an entire organ system?

pages.title: Part 1, Page 7: Body Cavities and Regions

content.text: The body has major cavities that house organs and protect them: the
cavities (dorsal body cavity, housing the brain and spinal cord), and the
cavities (ventral body cavity, housing the heart/lungs, digestive organs, and reproductive/urinary organs respectively).
Body regions further divide the body into named areas (e.g., abdominal quadrants) — a shared reference vocabulary that lets clinicians describe a location precisely without ambiguity.
Directional terms describe location relative to a standard reference position, and they're used constantly in setup documentation:
Toward the front / toward the back
Toward the head / toward the feet
Toward the midline / away from the midline
Closer to the trunk / farther from the trunk
Closer to the skin surface / farther from it
A lesion described as "medial to the nipple" is located:

options: Toward the midline of the body, relative to the nipple
Away from the midline of the body, relative to the nipple

content.text: Medial means toward the midline — the opposite, lateral, would mean away from the midline.
Body planes are imaginary flat surfaces used to describe cross-sectional views — the exact same planes you already work with in CT simulation and treatment planning:
— divides the body into left and right
— divides the body into anterior and posterior
— divides the body into superior and inferior
These aren't just anatomy-class vocabulary — they're literally the same three planes your CT/simulation and treatment planning images are reconstructed in.

pages.title: Part 1, Page 10: Transition to Oncology Terminology

content.text: You've now covered the general skeleton of medical language: word components, prefixes, suffixes, decoding real terms, body organization, directional terms, and planes. This vocabulary applies across every area of medicine.

From here, the lesson shifts to vocabulary that's specifically built around cancer diagnosis, treatment, and documentation — the terminology you'll actually be reading and writing daily as a radiation therapist.

pages.title: Part 2, Page 1: Why Oncology Has Its Own Vocabulary

content.text: Cancer diagnosis, treatment, and tumor registry documentation rely on a specialized set of word roots and suffixes layered on top of general medical terminology. This section draws on the U.S. National Cancer Institute's SEER Program tumor registrar training materials — a public resource specifically built to teach exactly this vocabulary.
The same rule applies here as in Part 1: you're not memorizing whole words, you're learning a smaller set of pieces that recombine constantly across cancer-related terms.

pages.title: Part 2, Page 2: The Core Tumor Roots

content.text: By itself, doesn't specify benign or malignant
The root carcin/o literally translates to which word?
Carcin/o comes from the Greek word for "crab" — the ancient association was the crab-like, spreading appearance of some tumors. Sarc/o is the one meaning "flesh."

pages.title: Part 2, Page 3: -oma vs. Carcinoma vs. Sarcoma

content.text: This distinction matters clinically, not just linguistically:
alone just means "tumor" — it doesn't say benign or malignant (e.g., a lipoma, a benign fatty tumor).
origin (skin, glands, linings of organs) — the most common category of cancer.
tissue origin (bone, muscle, fat, cartilage) — much less common than carcinoma, but distinct enough to always be named separately.
So "osteosarcoma" (oste/o = bone + sarcoma) is a malignant bone tumor, while "adenocarcinoma" (aden/o = gland + carcinoma) is a malignant tumor arising from glandular tissue.
These describe what a patient is experiencing — the complaints found in a history and physical:
These appear constantly in diagnoses and chart documentation:
A patient's chart notes "esophageal stenosis." What is happening to the esophagus?
-stenosis means narrowing/stricture — the opposite process, -ectasis, means expansion or dilation.

pages.title: Part 2, Page 6: Growth and Formation Terms

content.text: A cluster of related suffixes describe tissue growth patterns — and the differences between them matter enormously in oncology:

pages.title: Part 2, Page 7: Decoding Real Oncology Terms

content.text: Let's apply everything from this section to terms you'll actually see in a chart:
Break down "chondrosarcoma": chondr/o means cartilage. What does the full term mean?
Chondr/o (cartilage) + sarcoma (malignant connective-tissue tumor) = a malignant cartilage tumor.

pages.title: Part 2, Page 8: Abbreviations in Cancer Documentation

content.text: Beyond full terms, oncology charting relies heavily on standardized abbreviations — staging notation (T/N/M), grading (G1–G4), and treatment-related shorthand you'll see constantly in a chart. Getting comfortable reading these quickly is just as important as knowing the full-word vocabulary, since most day-to-day documentation uses the abbreviated form. (See the Medical Record Documentation lesson under Patient Care for how these fit into the treatment record itself.)

You've now covered both halves: the general word-building skeleton of medical language (Part 1), and the specialized vocabulary layered on top of it for oncology specifically (Part 2) — tumor roots, the carcinoma/sarcoma distinction, symptomatic and diagnostic suffixes, and growth/formation terminology.
